result.summary: A set of short, doubtful fragments attributed to Hesiod and quoted by ancient writers. They include lines on Athamas' madness, the Hesperides, a hymn-singing contest at Delos, the sons of Orchomenus, and Telemon's killing of Melanippe.

scenes.title: Scattered quoted fragments
scenes.summary: Single lines quoted by ancient authors, with no continuous narrative. Topics range from Zeus driving Athamas mad to Telemon slaying Melanippe.

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable proverb that gifts sway gods and princes, quoted by Plato.
Claims Hesiod and Homer jointly sang the first hymns at Delos.

analysis.text: These lines survive only as quotations by later writers, showing how ancient scholars and philosophers used Hesiodic verse and attributed doubtful lines to him.
The fragments touch divine power over mortals, the gods' susceptibility to gifts, and genealogy, all typical Hesiodic concerns.

fun_facts.text: Fragment 6 is quoted by Plato in the Republic, where he criticises the idea that gods can be bribed.

language_notes.text: Athamas, a legendary king of Boeotia, was driven mad by the gods; in myth he hunted his own son Learchus as a deer in his madness.
'Stitching song' translates a Greek image for composing poetry; singers were said to sew or stitch together verses.
The Hesperides were nymphs who guarded golden apples in the far west; the dots mark a gap in the quoted text.
Ocean's streams refers to the great river thought to encircle the world; mixing water with it suggests a ritual or drinking act.
Telemon, father of the greater Ajax, fought with Heracles against the Amazons; the 'golden-girdled queen' is Hippolyte, whose sister Melanippe he is said to have slain.

context_notes.text: These are fragments: single lines preserved only because later writers quoted them, so each lacks its original setting.
Delos was the island birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, and a major centre of Apollo's worship and of hymn-singing.
Plato quotes this line in the Republic to criticize the idea that gods can be bribed with gifts.
Orchomenus was a Boeotian city; Aspledon and Clymenus are named as its legendary founding family.

literary_notes.text: Song is likened to sewing cloth, presenting poetic composition as a craft of joining pieces into something new.
'Ox-eyed' is a stock descriptive epithet, here marking Hesperethusa as large-eyed and beautiful.
'Never sated with battle' and 'destroyer of men' characterize heroes and foes by their warlike nature in formulaic phrases.
